title: How Do I Get a Seat at the Table
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece examines the tension leaders face when high-performing team members push for a place in strategic decision-making. It argues that expanding the decision-making circle too far degrades quality, since more voices tend to produce more self-interest and complexity rather than better outcomes. The author's proposed fix is a distinction between input, which anyone can contribute, and advocacy, which is reserved for a smaller group tasked with reaching a final call. Well-designed input channels let ambitious contributors feel heard without diluting the decision itself. The piece closes by framing this as a structural design problem for leaders rather than a matter of favoritism or exclusion.
points: Team members who ask for a 'seat at the table' are usually asking to be heard, not necessarily to vote on the final decision.
Expanding the group of actual decision-makers past a small handful tends to produce slower, lower-quality outcomes driven by competing self-interest.
Leaders should separate 'input' (anyone can offer facts and views) from 'advocacy' (a limited group debates and decides).
Building deliberate channels for input, even without a seat at the final table, meaningfully reduces frustration among ambitious team members.
The best leaders reserve advocacy for those with the seniority and analytical skill to weigh competing facts under pressure.
quotes: In the contemporary organization of inclusion and consensus, leaders are bombarded by team members who want to participate in the decision-making that affects both them and the team.
Good leaders know that only so many people can be included in major decisions.
The best leaders solve this dilemma by distinguishing between input and advocacy within the organization and team.
Advocacy, on the other hand, is about actively staking out a position and persuading others to yield to this view.
Not everyone who wants to participate in a decision can be accommodated in most organizations.
Input and advocacy are different animals. Good leaders design decision-making processes accordingly.
